participants: Chris Klevan (Primal Instinct) — sales manager, runs call QC and team coaching
Referenced but not present: Kim (setter, KFS), Harry (closer), Brian (external sales trainer, mastery tier), Vishrant, Isaiah, Josh Lyons, Cole
summary: A roughly 23-minute manager one-to-one between Chris Klevan and Farooq Bey, opening with Farooq escalating a badly qualified booked call and Chris agreeing to review the set and give the setter, Kim, feedback. Chris then reports the results of his own call QC: several of Farooq's recent prospects were not financially qualified, and only one — Roy — was 'technically closeable'. Farooq's close rate is stated outright as 13%, and Chris explicitly tells him not to get in his head about it because he understands why it is there. The two then discuss whether Brandon should have been closed; Chris rules that he was not closeable and that the $1,200 'love it or leave it' must not be used on prospects with no path to keep paying. Roughly the last fifteen minutes leave sales entirely and become a discussion of consciousness work, ego dissolution, God and surrender, centred on the external trainer Brian and a teacher named Vishrant, whose programmes Farooq is paying for and not attending.
notable: Close rate stated on the record: 'Dude, 13% close rate. Right now, I'm very aware of why it's at that point. So don't get in your head about it.' This is the benchmark figure for this rep in this period and should anchor any close-rate rollup.

Management acknowledges a lead-qualification problem upstream rather than a closing problem: 'you've had quite a few prospects that weren't. Really financially qualified.' This independently corroborates the ICP findings across this batch, where nearly every prospect failed the income criterion.

STATED POLICY on the $1,200 product, from the manager: 'I don't want to put somebody on a love it or leave it for $1,200 if I just know they're going to default the month after. If there's no path for them to actually pay the payments after that... they get, what, a month out of it? They get started and then nothing. It's not worth it.' The rep had sold exactly that product the previous day to a prospect in active Chapter 7 bankruptcy.

The manager treats the 'love it or leave it' as an ordinary, unremarkable tool of the trade. The rep presents it to prospects as a rule-breaking favour — 'I'm not meant to really recommend this' and 'Typically I'm not meant to really offer this'.

MATERIAL CORRECTION TO THE SALES CORPUS: the Roy Norman call ends on the recording with an unambiguous verbal yes, immediately followed by the rep removing the Fathom notetaker. Here the rep describes what happened next: 'the Fathom, I took the Fathom out, we're about to pay, and that's when he was like, oh, paying now? I'm like, yeah, you just said you want to pay now. What's happening?' The manager treats Roy as an unconverted opportunity — 'he was the only one who was technically closeable because he had the funds' and 'there was probably something on that call that would have allowed him to close.' Roy did not pay.

Because this rep habitually stops recording at the moment of close, every deal he writes is unauditable from the recordings alone, and the Roy call proves the resulting bias exists and runs in one direction — recordings overstate conversion.

An escalation path for bad sets exists and is used: Farooq raised a mis-set call, Chris committed to listening to both the set and the closing call and to feeding back to Kim. Note the set is reviewed only after the closer complains, and against the closer's own assessment.

The rep told a prospect the previous day, 'I manage a team, there's two other guys under me. One is actually based in the States, in Pennsylvania, the other guy's based in Birmingham right now, but he's moving out to Brazil soon.' In this call he is the one being managed, QC'd and coached, and Chris says 'I have you on this team.' Worth verifying which is accurate.

The manager's coaching content in response to a 13% close rate was, in substance, 'I would continue to keep focusing on the training that we've been focusing on' and 'the deals will come. The right people will make their way.' No tactical feedback was given on discovery, the consequence frame or the commitment check, which are the phases failing consistently across this rep's calls.

Roughly two thirds of the call is spiritual and personal-development discussion — ego, surrender, God, loving strangers, Satsang — rather than sales performance. Recorded as an observation about how manager one-to-ones are spent, not as a criticism of the content.

The rep is paying for a 'mastery tier' with the external trainer Brian and not attending the calls; the manager instructs him to start using it. The rep says he intends to begin one-to-one coaching next month 'after I've just stacked a bit more cash.'

Manager's stated framing of employment risk, delivered unprompted: 'if at some point I feel that having your back means letting you go, because that's the best thing for your growth, then that's what it means.'
